title: Keys & joins: how tables point at each other
objectives: Choose between a surrogate (identity or UUID) and a natural primary key, knowing a key must not change and an identity has gaps
Pick the `ON DELETE` action for each foreign key (`CASCADE`, `SET NULL`, `RESTRICT`, the default `NO ACTION`) and index the referencing column yourself
Model one-to-many with a foreign key, and many-to-many with a join table whose composite primary key blocks duplicate links
Predict what `INNER` and `LEFT JOIN` return, including `count(*)` on a null-filled row, a `WHERE` that undoes a `LEFT JOIN`, and fan-out inflating a `sum`
Spot `NOT IN` returning nothing because of a `NULL`, and rewrite it with `NOT EXISTS`

sources.title: PostgreSQL 18 docs: Subquery Expressions (EXISTS, IN, NOT IN)

questions.prompt: The report is "every customer, with their number of orders — zero included". Which join from `customers` to `orders`?

options.text: `customers LEFT JOIN orders` — every customer appears, with `NULL` order columns when there's no match
`customers JOIN orders` — a join already includes every row of both tables
`customers RIGHT JOIN orders` — the orders side is the one that might be missing
No join can do this; it needs two separate queries

questions.explanation: An inner join keeps only rows that found a partner, so a customer with no orders vanishes from the report — the bug nobody notices because the remaining numbers look right. `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row of the left table and fills the right side with `NULL`. `RIGHT JOIN` keeps every *order*, which is the opposite of what's asked (and every order has a customer anyway).

questions.prompt: `users.email` is required and unique. Why do most schemas still give `users` a separate `id` primary key and make `email` just `UNIQUE`?

options.text: Emails change, and every foreign key stores a copy of the key it points at — so a change is refused, or (with `ON UPDATE CASCADE`) rewrites every referencing row
A `text` column can't be a primary key in PostgreSQL
A primary key on `email` wouldn't get an index, so lookups by email would be slow
Because `UNIQUE` is stronger than `PRIMARY KEY`, so `email` gets the better guarantee

questions.explanation: A natural key is fine as long as it never changes. Emails do, and the key's value is copied into `orders.user_id`, `sessions.user_id` and every other table that points at the user — by default PostgreSQL refuses the update while references exist. A meaningless surrogate never needs changing, and `UNIQUE` on `email` keeps the guarantee. Text primary keys are allowed and every primary key gets a unique B-tree index; `UNIQUE` plus `NOT NULL` is *functionally almost the same* as a primary key, not stronger.

questions.prompt: `tasks.assignee_id` references `users(id)`. When someone leaves and their user row is deleted, their tasks should stay on the board, unassigned. Which `ON DELETE` action?

options.text: `ON DELETE SET NULL` (with `assignee_id` nullable)
`ON DELETE CASCADE`
Nothing — the default handles it
`ON DELETE RESTRICT`

questions.explanation: Ask what should happen to the *child*. The task should survive with no owner, which is `SET NULL` — and the column must allow `NULL` for that to work. `CASCADE` would delete the person's tasks along with them: silent data loss. The default (`NO ACTION`) and `RESTRICT` both refuse to delete the user while any task still points at them, which is right for invoices but not here.

questions.prompt: You add `orders.customer_id bigint REFERENCES customers (id)`. Which index does PostgreSQL create because of that line?

options.text: None — `customers.id` is already indexed as its primary key, and the referencing column `orders.customer_id` gets no index unless you create one
An index on `orders.customer_id`, so the constraint can be checked
One on each side of the relationship
A unique index on `orders.customer_id`

questions.explanation: The referenced side must already be a primary key or unique (so it's indexed). The referencing side is left to you: the manual says a foreign key does not automatically create an index on the referencing columns. Without one, deleting a customer — or looking up a customer's orders — scans `orders`. A *unique* index there would be a bug: it would allow one order per customer.

questions.prompt: Students take many courses; courses have many students. How do you model it?

options.text: An `enrollments` table with `student_id` and `course_id` foreign keys and `PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)`
A `course_ids bigint[]` column on `students`
A `course_id` foreign key on `students`
A `course_id` on `students` and a `student_id` on `courses`

questions.explanation: Neither side can hold the relationship: a single `course_id` on `students` means one course per student. An array can hold many ids, but PostgreSQL can't put a foreign key on array elements, so nothing stops it pointing at a deleted course, and "who is in course 7?" means searching every array. A join table gives one row per link, a real foreign key on each side, a place for link data (`enrolled_at`, `grade`), and the composite key blocks enrolling the same student twice.

questions.prompt: `team_members` has `id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY`, plus `team_id` and `user_id` foreign keys — and no other constraint. What can go wrong?

options.text: The same user can be added to the same team twice; nothing makes `(team_id, user_id)` unique
Nothing — the primary key already makes each row unique
The foreign keys won't work, because a join table can't have its own `id`
Inserts fail once the identity sequence passes the number of users

questions.explanation: The surrogate `id` makes each *row* unique, but two rows `(id 1, team 7, user 3)` and `(id 2, team 7, user 3)` are different rows describing the same link — and the duplicate shows up as a doubled member in every count. Uniqueness has to be declared on the columns that define the link: `PRIMARY KEY (team_id, user_id)` or a `UNIQUE (team_id, user_id)` alongside the `id`.

questions.prompt: `FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.total > 20` — customers with no orders are missing from the result. Why?

options.text: `WHERE` runs after the join; for a customer with no orders `o.total` is `NULL`, `NULL > 20` isn't true, so the row is filtered out
A `LEFT JOIN` only keeps unmatched rows when there's no `WHERE` clause at all
The planner drops unmatched rows from any `LEFT JOIN` that has a `WHERE` clause, whatever the clause filters
It needs `LEFT OUTER JOIN`; plain `LEFT JOIN` is an inner join

questions.explanation: The manual: a restriction in `ON` is processed before the join, one in `WHERE` after it. The left join does add Linus with `NULL` order columns; then `WHERE o.total > 20` evaluates to `NULL` for him and throws the row away. Move the condition into the join (`ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 20`) to filter which orders *match* without filtering which customers *appear*. (`EXPLAIN` shows the planner noticing: with the filter in `WHERE` it plans a plain inner join, because the results are identical.) `LEFT JOIN` and `LEFT OUTER JOIN` are the same thing.

questions.prompt: `SELECT email FROM users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM invites)` returns no rows at all, though most users were never invited. `invites` has one row whose `user_id` is `NULL`. What's the fix?

options.text: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM invites i WHERE i.user_id = u.id)`
Swap `NOT IN` for `IN` and negate in the application
`NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM invites)`
`WHERE coalesce(id, 0) NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM invites)`

questions.explanation: `x NOT IN (1, NULL)` means `x <> 1 AND x <> NULL`; the second comparison is `NULL`, so the whole condition is never true and every row is filtered out. `NOT EXISTS` only asks whether the subquery returned a row, so a `NULL` can't poison it. `DISTINCT` keeps the `NULL`. Wrapping the *left* side in `coalesce` changes nothing — the `NULL` is on the right. (Adding `WHERE user_id IS NOT NULL` to the subquery also works, but `NOT EXISTS` is the habit that doesn't depend on remembering.)

prompts.prompt: A membership means nothing without its team: point `team_id` at `teams` and delete memberships along with their team.
prompts.code: team_id bigint NOT NULL ___ teams (id) ON DELETE ___,
prompts.explanation: `REFERENCES teams (id)` is the foreign key. `ON DELETE CASCADE` deletes referencing rows when the referenced row goes — right for a child that's meaningless alone, wrong for anything you'd want to keep (use `SET NULL` or `RESTRICT` there).

prompts.prompt: Make adding the same user to the same team twice an error.
code: team_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES teams (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
user_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
prompts.explanation: A composite `PRIMARY KEY (team_id, user_id)` (or `UNIQUE`) declares that the pair identifies the link, so a second identical pair fails with `23505`. Its index is ordered by `team_id` first, so it doesn't serve lookups by `user_id` — and PostgreSQL never indexes a foreign key's referencing column for you — hence the second index.

prompts.prompt: Every customer, paired with any order over 20 — customers without one still appear.
code: ___ JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id ___ o.total > 20;
prompts.explanation: The condition goes in `ON`, joined with `AND`, so it decides which orders match. Put it in `WHERE` instead and it runs after the join, where the null-filled rows fail it and the customers without a big order vanish.

prompts.prompt: Count each customer's orders and total spend so that a customer with no orders shows `0` and `0`, not `1` and `NULL`.
code: SELECT c.name, count(___) AS orders, ___(sum(o.total), 0) AS spent
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
prompts.explanation: `count(*)` counts rows, and the null-filled row the left join adds is a row — so it reports 1. `count(o.id)` counts non-null values: 0. `sum` over no values is `NULL`; `coalesce(…, 0)` turns that into 0. (`count(o.customer_id)` or `count(o.total)` work too: any column of `o` that is never `NULL` in a real row does.)

prompts.prompt: Users with no invite, written so a `NULL` in `invites.user_id` can't empty the result.
code: WHERE ___ (SELECT 1 FROM invites i WHERE i.user_id = u.id);
prompts.explanation: `EXISTS` is true if the subquery returns any row and false if it returns none — it never inspects the values, so it has no three-valued-logic trap. `NOT IN` against a list containing `NULL` is never true.

code: -- customers: Ada, Grace, Linus. orders: Ada has 2, Grace 1, Linus none.
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
snippets.question: What does the `orders` column say for Linus?
snippets.explanation: The `LEFT JOIN` gives Linus one row with every `o.` column `NULL`, and `count(*)` counts rows. `count(o.id)` counts non-null values and would say 0. This is the most common off-by-one in reporting queries: every customer with no orders is reported as having one.

code: WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM invites);
snippets.question: Which ids come back?
snippets.explanation: For id 2: `2 <> 1` is true, `2 <> NULL` is `NULL`, and `true AND NULL` is `NULL` — not true, so `WHERE` drops it. The same happens to every id. Most people predict `2, 3`. `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM invites i WHERE i.user_id = users.id)` returns `2, 3`.

code: -- order 1 has 3 line items worth 25 in total,
SELECT sum(i.qty * i.price) AS item_total, sum(p.amount) AS paid
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments p    ON p.order_id = o.id
snippets.question: What are `item_total` and `paid`?
snippets.explanation: The two joins produce one row per (item, payment) pair: 3 × 2 = 6 rows. Each item appears twice (25 → 50) and each payment three times (30 → 90). Aggregate each child in its own subquery (`GROUP BY order_id`) and join the one-row results. `sum(DISTINCT p.amount)` is not a fix: the two payments are both 15, so it would say 15.

code: -- customers.id is GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY; the last id handed out was 3.
INSERT INTO customers (name) VALUES ('Margaret') RETURNING id;
snippets.question: What id does Margaret get?
snippets.explanation: The rolled-back insert drew 4 from the identity's sequence, and the manual is explicit that a value from `nextval` is never reclaimed when the transaction aborts — so concurrent inserts never wait on each other. Failed inserts and `INSERT … ON CONFLICT` leave gaps too. Ids are unique, not consecutive: never count rows with `max(id)`, and never use a sequence for numbers that must be gap-free.
